qs.q: Polycythaemia vera is associated with which mutation in >95% of cases?
qs.e: JAK2 V617F causes constitutive activation of the JAK-STAT signalling pathway, driving erythroid (and myeloid) proliferation independent of EPO.

qs.q: Which of the following is a hallmark feature of polycythaemia vera?
o: Decreased total red blood cell mass
Low erythropoietin levels with increased haematocrit
Elevated erythropoietin due to systemic hypoxia
qs.e: In primary polycythaemia vera, autonomous marrow proliferation (driven by JAK2 mutation) raises red cell mass while suppressing EPO via negative feedback.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Polycythaemia vera is a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm causing excess red cells, often with raised platelets and white cells. Diagnosis relies on blood counts, low erythropoietin, and JAK2 mutation. Management aims to reduce thrombosis risk and control blood volume.

sections.p: PV is a clonal stem‑cell disorder that produces too many red cells, frequently accompanied by leukocytosis and thrombocytosis. Diagnosis requires meeting WHO criteria.
b: Hb > 16.5 g/dL (men) or > 16.0 g/dL (women) or Hct > 49% (men) / > 48% (women)
Low serum erythropoietin
Presence of JAK2 V617F or exon 12 mutation
Exclusion of secondary causes of erythrocytosis

t.b: Does the patient have erythrocytosis and possible leukocytosis/thrombocytosis? Elevated Hb/Hct confirms polycythaemia; high platelets suggest PV rather than secondary.
Is the erythropoietin suppressed? Low EPO supports primary over secondary erythrocytosis.
Is a JAK2 V617F or exon 12 mutation present? Positive result confirms clonal PV; if unavailable, rely on clinical criteria and bone marrow biopsy.
What is the marrow architecture? Shows pan‑myelosis with fibrosis early; used when mutation testing not feasible.

sections.p: PV severity is gauged by risk of thrombosis and disease phase (prefibrotic vs overt fibrotic).
b: Low‑risk: age < 60 y and no prior thrombosis
High‑risk: age ≥ 60 y or history of thrombosis
Advanced phase: development of myelofibrosis or blast transformation

sections.p: PV is a primary clonal disorder; secondary erythrocytosis must be excluded.
b: JAK2‑mutated clonal proliferation (most common)
Chronic hypoxia (e.g., COPD, high altitude) – secondary
Erythropoietin‑producing tumors (renal, hepatic) – secondary

sections.p: Patients often notice ruddy complexion, headaches, pruritus after hot showers, or thrombosis. Splenomegaly may be palpable.
b: Erythrocytosis‑related symptoms: headache, dizziness, visual disturbances
Pruritus, especially after warm baths
Thrombotic events: deep‑vein thrombosis, stroke, myocardial infarction
Mild splenomegaly

sections.p: Laboratory and imaging confirm diagnosis, assess risk, and rule out mimics.
b: CBC with differential
Serum EPO
JAK2 mutation assay
Abdominal ultrasound for splenomegaly

t.b: Is the spleen enlarged? Splenomegaly supports PV and helps monitor disease progression.

sections.p: Complications stem from hyperviscosity and clonal evolution.
b: Acute arterial or venous thrombosis
Progression to myelofibrosis
Blast phase acute leukemia
Hemorrhage from extreme platelet counts

sections.p: Therapy reduces blood viscosity, prevents thrombosis, and controls clonal proliferation.
b: Phlebotomy to keep Hct < 45% (men) / < 42% (women)
Low‑dose aspirin for platelet inhibition unless contraindicated
Cytoreductive agents (hydroxyurea) for high‑risk or progressive disease
Interferon‑α for younger patients or pregnancy

sections.p: Regular monitoring detects progression and guides therapy adjustments.
b: CBC every 3–6 months; Hct target as above
Annual assessment for fibrosis (bone marrow) if clinically indicated
Vaccination against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce infection‑related thrombosis
Lifestyle: smoking cessation, hydration, avoid iron deficiency

sections.p: Conditions that also cause erythrocytosis or splenomegaly.
b: Secondary polycythaemia from chronic hypoxia
Relative erythrocytosis due to dehydration
Chronic myeloid leukemia (leukocytosis dominant)
Essential thrombocythemia (platelet‑predominant)

sections.p: Certain labs may be falsely normal, leading to missed diagnosis.
b: Serum EPO can be normal in early PV; rely on JAK2 and marrow findings
Iron deficiency may mask high Hb; check iron studies if suspicion remains
Platelet count may be normal early; repeat CBC if symptoms persist

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe headache or visual loss
Chest pain or shortness of breath suggesting pulmonary embolism
Rapidly worsening leg swelling or pain indicating deep‑vein thrombosis

faq.q: Why is phlebotomy used in PV?
faq.a: It reduces hematocrit, lowering blood viscosity and thrombosis risk without medication.

faq.q: When is hydroxyurea preferred over interferon?
faq.a: In older or high‑risk patients where rapid cytoreduction is needed and interferon side‑effects are less tolerable.
No, it is a chronic disease; treatment controls symptoms and complications.
